result:
Solution 2 is the one that matches my derivation. I did not verify the time-scale claims rigorously; I checked them heuristically.

**Structure.** The tree is a spine (i,0) with a dead-end finger of length i attached at each (i,0). A cut time requires the step edge to be crossed exactly once. Finger edges are always crossed an even number of times, because the walk must come back out to escape to infinity. So only spine edges can be cut edges.

**Density of cut edges.** Ignoring finger excursions, the spine walk goes up with probability 1/(1+λ) and down with probability λ/(1+λ). The probability of never returning from i+1 to i is therefore 1−λ. By ergodicity, the density of cut spine edges is 1−λ almost surely.

**Time scale.** Inside finger i the walk drifts toward the tip, so the time to return to the spine is of order λ^{-i}. Each spine vertex is visited O(1) times on average, and a deep excursion happens with constant probability per visit. Hence T_n, the time to reach level n, satisfies log T_n / n → log(1/λ). The maximum level reached by time N is then about log N / log(1/λ).

**Combining.** M(N) ≈ (1−λ) · log N / log(1/λ), so the limit is (1−λ)/(−log λ).

**Checking the other solutions.**
- Solution 1 claims that nearly every spine level is a cut level, ignoring that the spine walk returns to earlier levels with probability λ. This overcounts by the factor 1−λ.
- Solution 3 concludes the limit is 0 by dividing by N instead of log N, which is the wrong normalization.

CHOICE: 2
